title: Madras High Court Upholds OCI Cancellation Over Unauthorised Missionary Preaching
excerpt: Justice D. Bharatha Chakravarthy ruled that US citizen John Daniel needed special permission under the March 4, 2021 notification before preaching in India, even without any conversion, and upheld the September 4, 2026 cancellation of his OCI registration.
body:
• The Madras High Court dismissed US citizen John Daniel's petition and upheld the September 4, 2026 cancellation of his OCI registration over missionary activities in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh.
  • Justice D. Bharatha Chakravarthy held that OCI cardholders need special permission under notification S.O.1050(E) of March 4, 2021 before preaching or missionary work, even if no religious conversion is involved.
  • The court rejected Daniel's claim that he visited India only to see his 92-year-old mother, calling the denial, on the materials produced, "on its face a lie."
  • For OCI holders: check the permission list before any missionary, Tabligh, mountaineering or journalistic activity in India, or a visit to a protected or restricted area.

The Madras High Court has upheld the cancellation of a United States citizen's Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) registration, ruling that preaching religion in India counts as missionary activity and requires special permission in advance, whether or not any conversion takes place.

Justice D. Bharatha Chakravarthy dismissed a writ petition filed by John Daniel challenging the September 4, 2026 order of the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer-cum-Civil Authority, which cancelled his OCI registration under Sections 7D(da) and 7D(e) of the Citizenship Act, 1955. Daniel, whose parents were of Indian origin, was granted OCI registration on February 6, 2015, according to LawBeat's report of the judgment.

What the court decided

The court held that notification S.O.1050(E), dated March 4, 2021 and issued under Section 7B of the Citizenship Act, requires an OCI cardholder to obtain special permission or a special permit from the competent authority, the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer or the Indian Mission concerned before undertaking missionary, mountaineering or journalistic activities. Carrying on missionary activity without that permission violates Section 7B and makes the registration liable to cancellation under Section 7D(da), the court said, in reasoning reported by Verdictum.

https://x.com/MeghUpdates/status/2115763501918720130
"It is not only for conversion, but even to be a missionary preaching his religion, it is only a prior permission that is mandated."

If a petitioner preaches to spread the word of God, the judge added, that falls within missionary activity and permission ought to have been obtained. Daniel had not obtained it, so the cancellation stood justified.

The allegations and the denial

A show-cause notice issued in September 2025 alleged that Daniel had misused his OCI status, preaching in villages in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, organising prayer meetings and encouraging Christian conversions. It also alleged that he led the Laymen's Evangelical Fellowship International, which the authorities described as functioning like a cult. The Union produced posters and advertisements for religious meetings between 2017 and 2019, including his speeches at LEF Church in Tenali, Andhra Pradesh, in January 2017.

Daniel denied the allegations. He said he visited India to meet and attend to his 92-year-old mother, his sister, cousins and other relatives, and had neither engaged in missionary activity nor promoted conversions. He also argued that he had not been given the material relied on against him, and relied on the Delhi High Court's judgment in Ashok Swain v. Union of India and Others.

The court rejected that argument. Natural justice, it held, is not a straight-jacket formula and depends on the facts of each case. Daniel had not disputed any specific incident but had denied missionary activity altogether — a statement contradicted by substantial material showing he had consistently addressed congregations in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh, with advertisements inviting the public to attend. Those materials could not be regarded as fabricated or concocted, the judge observed. Live Law's report records the same reasoning.

What this means for OCI cardholders

The ruling matters beyond this case. An OCI card gives a multiple-entry lifelong visa to visit India, but not an unrestricted right to work in sensitive fields. Under the March 4, 2021 notification, as reported when it was issued by ANI, a special permit is required for missionary or Tabligh activities, mountaineering and journalistic activities, and to visit a protected, restricted or prohibited area notified by the Central Government. The court has now confirmed that preaching alone triggers that requirement, and that a breach can cost the cardholder the registration itself.

For diaspora visitors, the practical point is procedural: permission must come first, from the Foreigners Regional Registration Officer or the Indian Mission concerned.

What happens next

The petition was dismissed with no order as to costs. Daniel remains free to apply for a regular visa to visit his mother, and may conduct religious meetings in India only after obtaining the requisite permission. The case is John Daniel v. Union of India and Others, W.P. No. 37464 of 2026, neutral citation 2026:MHC:4303. Senior Counsel R. Shanmuga Sundaram appeared for Daniel; Senior Panel Counsel Dr S. Padma appeared for the Union.
